model_answer: Cognitive dissonance is the mental discomfort people experience when they hold two conflicting beliefs. The concept was introduced by the psychologist Leon Festinger in the 1950s. According to his theory, people are strongly motivated to reduce this discomfort. They may do so by changing one of their beliefs, by adding new beliefs, or by reducing the importance of the conflict. For example, a smoker who knows that smoking is harmful might decide that the health risks have been exaggerated.

model_answer: The theory of comparative advantage is one of the central ideas in international economics. It was developed by the British economist David Ricardo in the early nineteenth century. Ricardo argued that countries can benefit from trade even if one country produces everything more efficiently than another. What matters is the relative cost of production. If each country specializes in the goods it produces at the lowest opportunity cost, total output increases, and both trading partners can be better off.

model_answer: Linguists estimate that roughly seven thousand languages are spoken in the world today. However, many of them are in danger of disappearing. A language becomes endangered when children no longer learn it from their parents. This often happens when a community shifts toward a more dominant language that offers better economic opportunities. When the last fluent speakers die, valuable knowledge about local plants, history, and ways of thinking may be lost forever.
